sites.reasoning: The dead thing on this line is not a branch or a clause — it is the third argument of `Keyword.get(case_meta, :line, 1)`. The line itself is live: it runs on every successful hoist, and `test/semantic/fix_case_branch_assignment_scope_fix_test.exs` exercises it 11 times. Only the fallback constant `1` is unreachable, because `case_meta` is always the meta of a `:case` node that came straight out of `Sourceror.parse_string/1` (the pattern `{:case, case_meta, [subject, branches_kw]} = case_stmt` only ever binds a parsed node; the prewalk's first clause is guarded on `acc == false` and the accumulator is monotone false->true, so the synthesized case is never re-fed to `hoist_case_assignment/3`). I confirmed independently that a parser-produced `:case` node always carries `:line`. Deleting the dead default means replacing `Keyword.get/3` with `Keyword.fetch!/2` (KeyError) or `case_meta[:line]` (emits `[line: nil]` into the AST that `Sourceror.to_string/1` then renders). Neither is an improvement: this call sits inside `fix/2`, which has NO rescue, and `should_report?/2` invokes `fix/2` during the analyze phase — so a raise here would abort an analysis run rather than degrade gracefully. This is the textbook defensive default: currently unreachable, cheap, and its removal trades a safe line number for a crash if Sourceror's meta invariant ever shifted. Keep it.

sites.reasoning: Same shape, twice on one line: `err_line >= Keyword.get(start, :line, 0) and err_line <= Keyword.get(finish, :line, 0)`. Note the two paths that would otherwise produce a key-less endpoint are already handled above this line: `get_range` returning `nil` falls to the `_ -> false` clause, and a raise inside it is caught by the function's `rescue _ -> false`. So the defaults only cover the residual case of a well-formed `%Sourceror.Range{}` with a `:line`-less endpoint, which Sourceror 1.12 does not produce. Deleting them is not a no-op even in principle: with `Keyword.fetch!` a missing start key would raise into the rescue and yield `false`, whereas the current default `0` makes the start bound vacuously satisfied and lets the finish bound decide — so the removal would change the hypothetical answer from 'spans' to 'does not span'. It is unreachable today either way, but it is a deliberate conservative default in the one predicate that decides whether the rewrite is safe to apply at all. Defensive default: keep.

The dead thing on line 162 is only the *floor* of `max(depth - 1, 0)` in `entry_start/3` — not the branch and not the decrement. The ledger confirms that scoping: at line 162 the mutant `depth - 1` -> `depth - 2` (col 55) SURVIVED as a real GAP, and `max(_, 1)` (col 58, 0 -> 1) was KILLED by 3 tests, so the opener branch runs and `depth - 1` genuinely reaches 0. Only `max(_, 0)` -> `max(_, -1)` survives, i.e. the clamp never engages.

Why it never engages: `locate/1` line 142 requires `{:ok, opener_at, ?{} <- SourceMask.enclosing_opener(shadow, comma_at)` BEFORE calling `entry_start/3` at line 144, on the same `shadow` binding. `enclosing_opener/2` (lib/source_mask.ex:199-215) walks `(comma_at - 1)..0//-1` with byte-for-byte the same classification (`[?), ?], ?}]` -> depth+1, `[?(, ?[, ?{]` -> depth-1) and HALTS on the first opener it meets at depth 0. Since it halted at `opener_at`, every opener strictly inside `(opener_at, comma_at - 1]` was seen at depth >= 1 — and that interval is exactly `entry_start/3`'s range. So `depth - 1 >= 0` at every opener the clamp could apply to, and the floor is unreachable. This matches the triage argument, so the triage is correct.

But this is a defensive floor whose deadness is a CROSS-MODULE contract, not a local one. Nothing in this file states or enforces it; it is a halt property of `SourceMask.enclosing_opener/2` in another module, and this rule is its only caller in lib/ (the only other reference is test/source_mask_test.exs:496). If that helper ever changes — stops halting at depth 0, gains a bracket class, or is given a range it did not certify — the floor becomes live again. And the failure mode of removing it is not a crash: depth goes negative, the `depth == 0` comma test at line 163 can then never fire, `entry_start` silently returns a different byte offset, and that offset is fed straight to `arrow_ify/3`, which does raw `binary_part` splicing into the user's source. That is a silent wrong-place edit, the exact class of defect this codebase keeps finding. I demonstrated the divergence is real and observable, not theoretical: on shadow `"%{,(,"` with `comma_at = 4`, the clamped version returns 3 and the unclamped returns 2 — the only reason no input gets there is that `enclosing_opener/2` reports `{:ok, 3, ?(}` for that position, which `locate/1` rejects.

So: deleting it removes no code (it is a 9-character wrapper, not a duplicated clause), removes no complexity, and trades a safe clamped default for a silent mis-splice if an invariant owned by a different module ever moves. That is the textbook KEEP shape. There is also a twin `max(depth - 1, 0)` at line 182 in `key_colon/3` scanning forward over a region that `enclosing_opener/2` does NOT certify — the sweep sampled 39 mutants and never generated one there, so nothing shows that twin is dead. Deleting one of the matched pair would leave an asymmetry that reads as an oversight.

sites.reasoning: Line 135 is `defp overlaps?({as, al, _, _}, {bs, bl, _, _}), do: as < bs + bl and bs < as + al` — a standard half-open-interval overlap test. There is no dead *branch* here and nothing to delete. The triage entry is narrow and correct, but it is about a boundary value, not about unreachable code: only the `<`->`<=` swap on the FIRST conjunct (col 58) is equivalent, because the case `as == bs + bl` (kernel_start == infix_end) is unreachable. That mechanism holds: @kernel_pattern `Kernel\s*\.\s*\/\/` always begins on the literal byte `K` (a \w byte), while @infix_pattern `(\w+)\s*\/\/\s*(\w+)` ends in a greedy trailing `\w+` with nothing after it in the pattern, so no backtracking can shorten it and the byte at infix_end is EOS or a non-\w byte. A 200k randomized fuzz over {K,e,r,n,l,.,/,_,a,b,1,2,space,tab,newline,0x01,%,\",?,0xC8} produced 0 pairs with kernel_start == infix_end. Both conjuncts are nonetheless fully live and load-bearing. `overlaps?` returns true on the documented shape `a // Kernel.//(b)` (kernel [5,14), infix [0,11)) — the real module returns "a // div(b)", i.e. the infix match is dropped. And conjunct 1's FALSE outcome is what keeps a disjoint later kernel match from being treated as an overlap: on `a // b + Kernel.//(c, d)` the matches are infix [0,6) and kernel [9,18); `as < bs + bl` is `9 < 6` = false, so the pair is non-overlapping and the real module returns "div(a, b) + div(c, d)". Delete conjunct 1 and the surviving `bs < as + al` is `0 < 18` = true, so the infix match would be wrongly rejected and that line would come back as "a // b + div(c, d)" — an uncorrected parse error. So the conjunct is not removable duplication; it is one half of a correct interval predicate whose equality case this caller happens not to be able to produce. That is exactly the 'defensive but currently unreachable boundary' shape: keep it. Separately, the second mutant on the same line (col 75, second conjunct) is classified GAP, not equivalent — I reproduced its separating input against the compiled rule: fix("x = Kernel.//n // 2") == "x = divdiv(n, 2)" today, and the `<=` mutant would yield "x = divn // 2". That is a missing test, not dead code, and it is further proof line 135 must stay.
